title: Pickpockets: Artists or Crooks?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore pickpocketing as a historical and modern crime, starting with a sidekick-origin banter tied to Oliver Twist-era London pickpocket slang. They cover why pickpocketing is seen as an "art," common crowd and distraction tricks (the sandwich, the stall and hook, fake bird droppings, mustard squirt, staged fights, the stroke), pickpocket hierarchy from cannons and Fagins to bag workers, lush workers and fob workers, child pickpockets, and prevention tips such as money belts, dummy wallets, and copies of documents. They discuss why pickpocketing has declined in the US (less cash, card security, cameras, felony penalties, fewer Fagins), its persistence in Europe, and the entry of Romania and Bulgaria into the EU. The episode ends with listener mail from a Kalamazoo listener who discovered kleptomania through an earlier episode, and a sign-off asking listeners to share revelations.

segments.title: Opening banter and sidekick origin
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about the show's start and Josh's intro about the word sidekick, which he traces to pickpocket slang in old London, where the side pocket was the safest spot.

segments.title: Pickpocketing as an art and types of opportunists
segments.summary: They frame pickpocketing as a criminal art, mention Bob Arnold, a professional who poses as a tourist to study pickpockets, and describe opportunistic thieves who target distracted people with open bags, sleeping beach-goers, and laptops in coffee shops.

segments.title: Why pickpocketing is non-confrontational and its penalties
segments.summary: They discuss why pickpocketing appeals to criminals: it is non-confrontational and usually involves no weapons. Penalties were historically small but many states now treat it as a felony. Victims often never know who took their wallet.

segments.title: Crowded subway sandwich scam and pickpocket teams
segments.summary: The sandwich scam is explained: a stall stops short in front of the mark while a hook bumps the mark from behind. Organized groups called cannons are led by an older Fagin who trains younger pickpockets, named after the Oliver Twist character.

segments.title: Pickpocket ranks: bag, lush and fob workers and child pickpockets
segments.summary: They describe lower-tier thieves: bag workers who target purses, lush workers who rob drunk subway riders, and fob workers who use two fingers to pull small change, with one estimate of four hundred dollars per subway ride. They also mention children used as pickpockets, often while begging.

segments.title: Distraction ploys: bird droppings, mustard, staged fights, the stroke
segments.summary: The hosts describe distraction tricks in which thieves fake bird droppings, squirt mustard or ketchup, stage fights, or pretend someone is drowning. They warn that false alarms about pickpockets can make victims reveal where their wallet is, and describe the stroke, where a thief feels for a bulge first.

segments.title: Pickpocket prevention and travel tips
segments.summary: Advice includes staying aware, avoiding back pockets, using money belts, locking zippers, carrying a dummy wallet, keeping copies of documents and a list of card numbers, and not carrying a Social Security card. Josh admits he wore a money belt in Europe.

segments.title: Decline of pickpocketing in the US and Europe
segments.summary: They cite reasons for the decline in US pickpocketing: less cash, card security, cameras, harsher felony penalties, and fewer Fagins. Crime statistics fell from about 23,000 reported cases to under 5,000, and the numbers are no longer tracked. Pickpocketing persists in Europe, and Romania and Bulgaria's EU entry is linked to a resurgence. They also touch on Times Square's cleanup.

segments.title: Listener mail: kleptomania confession
segments.summary: A listener from Kalamazoo, Michigan, writes that an earlier episode on kleptomania named her long-running compulsion to steal silverware. She plans to tell her therapist and apologize to local businesses.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact information
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck invite listeners to share revelations on Twitter, Facebook, or email, point to HowStuffWorks for more, and close the show.
